compression.title: Eclipse (eclipsearchive.org)
compression.lede: is an online archive of facsimiles of small-press and experimental writing, started in 2002 by Craig Dworkin and edited with Danny Snelson, whose author index holds co-written, edited and translated titles under their collaborators, editors and translators, names as printed.

sentences.text: Eclipse is an online archive of small-press and experimental writing at eclipsearchive.org, which names itself twice on its home page, Eclipse and ECLIPSE, and opens on two ways in, an index of authors and an index of titles.
It holds 20th-century small-press writing and 21st-century born-digital publications, and its centre is digital facsimiles of radical small-press writing from the last quarter of the 20th century.

Craig Dworkin is its Founding Editor and Danny Snelson its Editor; Dworkin, a poet, critic and Professor of English at the University of Utah, co-manages it with Snelson, assistant professor of English at UCLA, and Eclipse's site carries a page for Dworkin that lists him as Founding Senior Editor of Eclipse and opens on his scholarly books.

The authorship census admits it as an aggregator, a resource that gathers many works and says what it holds, files it under avant-garde and experimental archives and under collective and distributed authorship, and stands it to the census as infrastructure, its evidence facsimile, catalogue and primary text.

Dworkin started Eclipse in 2002 to give readers and scholars access to avant-garde works that were no longer in print from their original publishers, and Eclipse later expanded to publish selected new works and born-digital publications in the spirit of those presses.
The name is an homage to Douglas Messerli's Sun & Moon press, which keeps this Eclipse apart from the other uses of the word.
It is active: the home page announces a new item without a date.

Each included text is held as high-resolution scans of every page, most from Dworkin's personal collection, which the encyclopedia gives in Dworkin's words as an attempt to "conserve ... the facture and material specificity of the book or printed document as an object."

Eclipse is thus no publisher of record for the original presses, since it holds facsimiles of their publications, no rights holder by any statement in its saved pages, and no reading-copy edition, since it scans every page to conserve the printed object.

Its holdings are small-press books, pamphlets, magazines and periodical runs, among them L=A=N=G=U=A=G=E, Roof, This, Hills, Tottel's, Joglars and Big Allis, predominantly from North American presses, with translations and with titles in their original languages such as Joaquín Pasos's Poemas de un joven que no sabe inglés.

The newest item is the first issue of the fugitive Gnome Baker magazine, from October 1976, edited by Madeleine Burnside and Andrew W. Kelly, with work by Michael Davidson, Rita Myers and Michael Palmer.

The author index runs alphabetically from Emily Abendroth to Suzanne Zavrian, with a link to browse by title, and its unit is a title listed under its author or authors, with co-authors, editors and translators marked.

A co-written title stands under each collaborator: LEGEND appears under Bruce Andrews with Charles Bernstein, Ray DiPalma, Steve McCaffery and Ron Silliman named in brackets, and again under DiPalma and under McCaffery with the others named, and eXcLa stands under both Andrews and Maggie O'Sullivan, each entry naming the other.

Editors are credited in three notations: a bracket after the title, as L=A=N=G=U=A=G=E under Andrews and under Bernstein and Roof, Hills, Tottel's and This under theirs; a parenthesis after the name, as The Difficulties under Tom Beckett and Big Allis under both Jessica Grim and Melanie Neilson; and once a credit inside another entry, The Syntactic Revolution under Abraham Lincoln Gillespie, marked "[Ed. Richard Milazzo]".

A magazine issue devoted to one author stands under that author and under its editor: Big Sky Number Three under Clark Coolidge, with Bill Berkson credited as editor, and under Berkson as the "Clark Coolidge issue".
A translation stands under its translator as well as its author, so that Rosmarie Waldrop, marked "(trans.)", holds three titles that also stand under Helmut Heißenbüttel.

The archive reads the index as distributed authorship held without collapse, every collaborator, editor and translator holding the title under an entry of their own so that no single attribution absorbs the others; the authorial function is distributed across the index, and Eclipse's own responsibility for selection and rights is unstated.
Two saved entries run otherwise: the name Richard Milazzo occurs only inside Gillespie's entry, with no entry of its own, and Sandra and Ben Doller hold Sonneteers under one joint heading.
Names stand in the index as printed, initials included, as "P. Inman" and "T. R. Uthco", and the index lists All Saints under "Craig Dworkin" and L≠A≠N≠G≠U≠A≠G≠E under "Daniel Scott Snelson".

Its saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, so whether a printed name is a chosen name, a pen name or a group is not shown, and the facsimiles themselves are unread.

The archive's distinction for that unanswered case is that a pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function, while a heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself.

The census asks of Eclipse which authors, co-authors, editors and translators a small-press title is held under, within its question of how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed.

In the archive's account of heteronymy, the credits such an index records fall at its boundary: ordinary translation, where the translator's authorial function is not distinct from the translation role, and ordinary editing, where the editor's contribution is supportive, are typically not heteronymic, and not every case of distributed authorial substrate is heteronymic.

The same account sets legal accountability against exhaustive authorial identity, holds that heteronymy keeps responsibility from being confused with sole origination where a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution, and holds that the heteronymic architecture makes a reduction to one name register as loss.
What Eclipse answers is whether it holds a facsimile of a named small-press title and under which authors, editors and translators, and which titles a named author co-wrote or edited.

The account of its purpose, date and method is the encyclopedia's, since Eclipse's own pages state no purpose, selection, permissions or rights: its About page returned "The requested URL was not found on this server", and its licence and the number of titles it holds are not stated.

Its holder is Eclipse and its editors, the scans mostly from Dworkin's collection, with no rights terms in the saved pages; access is a free public website with the two indexes, and the title index was left unread.

In the archive's restatement of Bourdieu's field of restricted production, small-press publication is the first step by which the avant-garde is consecrated, followed by academic uptake, curricular inclusion and canonical status, and the archive notes that this analysis presumes consecration eventually arrives.

The archive places the facsimile in a generation-old turn that rehabilitates the manuscript as image, with Susan Howe's argument "that the archive's material particulars are the poem's body and not its packaging", works that solved for the human reader "how to publish the hand without dissolving it into type".

Its editors join it to neighbouring archives: Dworkin curates The UbuWeb Anthology of Conceptual Writing, Snelson is a senior editor of PennSound, and Jacket2 published an interview with Dworkin that the encyclopedia cites on Eclipse, while Jacket2 reissues Roof, which Eclipse lists under James Sherry.

The encyclopedia has no article on Eclipse: its title "Eclipse Archive" redirects to the section Eclipse of the article on Craig Dworkin, edited last on 1 November 2026, whose infobox gives eclipsearchive.org as his website.

Its disambiguation page for Eclipse lists Eclipse Comics, an American comic book publisher, and Eclipse (software), a software development platform, among the uses of the name, and does not list Eclipse.

Four other entities answer to the name and stay distinct from Eclipse: the Eclipse Foundation's archives, which keep the Eclipse Project's archived builds and collect each archived project's downloads, source and website into a single TGZ file; the apparel brand Eclipse Archives, whose shop lists an "ECLIPSE X JJK DROP" and whose TikTok profile has 71.1K followers; the High Altitude Observatory's archive of research-quality images of solar eclipses back to 1869, presented on NASA's eclipse site; and two Eclipse Marketplace plugins for archive files in the Eclipse IDE, the Archive Utility and a Zip archive editor.

At the name, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed a disambiguation on 1 November 2026, and the Capture Registry's innocent reading is that, given a name shared by a software foundation, a clothing brand, a solar image archive and IDE plugins, the Overview lists the senses it finds and asks which one is meant.

The Registry finds the poetry archive leading the list with one bullet and one card of eight, its two editors named at their grain without an institution and its newest item correct, and it reads "a digital poetry publisher and archive" as agreeing with the encyclopedia's account of the later expansion.

Absent from that composition, in the Registry's findings, are the 2002 start and its purpose, the facsimile form, the name's homage and the author index that holds each collaborator and translator under a name of their own, the card's snippet showing only the navigation "Eclipse ECLIPSE Authors Titles".

CAP-1-10.quote: The innocent reading first. Given a two-word name shared by a software foundation, a clothing brand, a solar image archive and IDE plugins, the Overview lists the senses it finds and asks which one the user means.

CAP-1-01.quote: 'ECLIPSE ARCHIVE' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE POETRY ARCHIVE ONE SENSE OF FIVE, ITS EDITORS AT THEIR GRAIN; ITS FACSIMILE PURPOSE, ITS DATE AND ITS AUTHOR INDEX NOT CARRIED

CAP-1-02.quote: THE ARCHIVE ONE SENSE OF FIVE. The poetry archive leads the list ('Poetry & Digital Archives') and holds one bullet and one card of eight;

CAP-1-04.quote: THE EDITORS AT THEIR GRAIN. 'founded by Craig Dworkin and edited by Danny Snelson' stands as the home page has it: 'Founding Editor: Craig Dworkin Editor: Danny Snelson'.

CAP-1-05.quote: such as Gnome Baker magazine' is the home page's one notice: 'NEW TO THE ARCHIVE: The first issue of the fugitive Gnome Baker magazine, from October, 1976.

CAP-1-12.quote: Both editors named; no institution; the archive's home page carded once among seven other Eclipse sources.

CAP-1-13.quote: The archive reached in one bullet of five senses of the name, with its editors and its newest item; the other four bullets and seven of eight cards are other Eclipse archives.

CAP-1-06.quote: PUBLISHER AND ARCHIVE, WITHOUT ITS PURPOSE. 'a digital poetry publisher and archive' agrees with Wikipedia's account, which the census holds: 'Eclipse later expanded to publish selected new works and born-digital publications in the spirit of those earlier presses.'

CAP-1-07.quote: The same sentence's first half is absent from the composition: 'Dworkin started the archive in 2002 to provide readers and scholars with access to avant-garde works that were no longer available in print from their original publishers'. So are the facsimile form ('high-resolution scans of every page of its included texts, most from Dworkin's personal collection') and the name's homage to 'Douglas Messerli ’s Sun & Moon press'.

CAP-1-08.quote: THE AUTHOR INDEX NOT CARRIED. The census reads Eclipse for its index, where a co-written title stands under every collaborator

CAP-1-09.quote: The card's snippet opens on the site's navigation, 'Eclipse ECLIPSE Authors Titles', and the composition gives no account of it.

CAP-1-11.quote: A disambiguation in which the poetry archive leads, its editors and newest item correct. Its purpose, its 2002 start and the author index that holds each collaborator and translator under a name of their own are not in the composition.
